newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kuchma says France reassuring over Chernobyl aid.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma says France reassuring over Chernobyl aid.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said on Friday that President Jacques Chirac's pledges to ensure Kiev gets funds to close the Chernobyl nuclear power plant had soothed his "bad mood" over the pace of Western aid.

Kuchma told a news conference he was "satisfied" by Chirac's assurances and expressed hopes that "the problems of Chernobyl might be solved" at talks of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations in Washington in February.
Earlier, he said he had "come to France in a bad mood over the problems" of Chernobyl.

Ukraine has promised to close Chernobyl, site in 1986 of the world's worst nuclear accident, by the year 2000. But it has accused the G7 of dragging its feet in providing a promised $3.1 billion in grants and credits to fund the shutdown.
Some Kiev diplomats suspect France of blocking the aid.
Chirac told Kuchma on Thursday he would be "very active" to ensure the aid plan was implemented, especially to complete construction of alternative power plants at Rovno and Khmelnitsky.

Kuchma reiterated calls for closer ties with NATO and said Kiev should be consulted, like Russia, on the Alliance's plans to expand eastwards. Ukraine wants guarantees that nuclear weapons will not be stationed in central or eastern Europe.

Enlargement "cannot go ahead without taking account of the interests of Russia and Ukraine," he told the news conference before leaving for the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, at the weekend.
But he said that, unlike Russia, Ukraine did not oppose NATO expansion. "Ukraine sees no threat from NATO because it is an alliance of democratic, civilised states," he said.

He said he and Chirac discussed Chirac's planned trip on Sunday to visit Russian President Boris Yeltsin near Moscow where he is recovering from pneumonia. Kuchma praised Yeltsin despite a feud over control of the ex-Soviet Black Sea fleet.

Kuchma said he was "very interested in (Yeltsin's) good health, because over the past five years the Russian President has shown himself to be a very very reasonable politician in relations between Russia and Ukraine."
He said he believed the countries would have signed a stalled Friendship Treaty by now had Russia not staged presidential elections last year.

He told the French business association CNPF that Kiev was placing top priority on developing its energy sector, followed by agriculture, and said French businesses were playing an "insufficient" role in the country.

"French industrial and economic interests are perhaps the least present, compared to Americans, Germans and others," he said, adding that French investors perhaps still "viewed Ukraine through the prism of relations with Russia".
French investments make up just two percent of a total of $1.23 billion of foreign investments in 1996, well behind the United States on 17.8 percent and Germany's 14.4 percent, the CNPF said.
